about.title: Jackson Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Jackson's small-town footprint along Highway 49 and Highway 88 means many falls happen in familiar places — a grocery store on Main Street, a motel near the highway junction, or a business lot uneven with age. Under California law, a property owner isn't automatically at fault just because someone fell; you generally have to show the owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn about it. That's why what happens right after a fall matters so much: photos of the spill, ice, or broken step, names of witnesses, and a request that any surveillance footage be preserved before it's erased. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves — we're a free service that connects you with an independent attorney in our network who can evaluate your fall, help gather evidence, and explain your options in plain terms, all on a contingency basis so there's no upfront cost.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Your Fall

items.title: Notice Is the Whole Case
items.desc: California requires proof the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help identify evidence — cleaning logs, prior complaints, or inspection records — that speaks to notice.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many stores and complexes overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to send a preservation request can be the difference between having proof and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, so even if you're found partly responsible for not seeing a hazard, you may still recover a reduced amount. An attorney can help present your side clearly.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Jackson?
items.answer: California generally gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If a government-owned property in Amador County is involved, the deadline can be much shorter, sometimes just months, so it's worth checking early.

items.question: What if I fell at a business along Highway 49 or Highway 88?
items.answer: Businesses along Jackson's main corridors still owe visitors the same duty to address known hazards. The evidence often centers on whether staff knew about a spill, ice, or uneven pavement and had a reasonable chance to fix or warn about it.

items.question: Will I have to prove the owner was careless?
items.answer: You'll generally need to show the owner knew or should have known about the dangerous condition and failed to address it. This is different from just proving you fell — documentation and witness accounts help build that connection.
